strengths: The paper provides a clear and operational diagnostic (partitioned class-conditional entropy and its temporal derivative) that connects the statistical-physics picture of speciation (Biroli et al., 2024) to a quantity that can actually be estimated in trained diffusion models; this bridges a real gap between theory and practice acknowledged in the related work.

The theoretical analysis is self-contained and careful: the derivation of the entropy production rate (Eq. 8, Appendix A.1) via the Fokker–Planck equation is clean, and the asymptotic analysis correctly identifies the logarithmic speciation time scale t_s = ½ log d for VP and explains why VE/EDM lacks a sharp transition (Appendix A.2.3, Figure 5).

The guidance analysis (Figure 3) is a genuinely interesting empirical finding: guidance restricted to FID-optimal vs. FD_DINOv2-optimal intervals redistributes entropy production in qualitatively different ways, providing a mechanistic-complementary view of the limited-interval guidance results of Kynkäänniemi et al. (2024).

Experimental details are reasonably complete (sampler, NFE, sample counts, grid-search tables for guidance settings), and the limitations section is honest about estimator bias, the unconditional-model proxy for class complements, and the restricted scale of the models studied.
The failure-case analysis in Appendix C.2 (Figure 16) and the discussion of when the metric does not reflect the intended attribute add credibility rather than overselling.
weaknesses: The main theoretical result is largely a re-derivation of the known speciation time of Biroli et al. (2024) in a Gaussian mixture with entropy as the observable; the novelty of the VP result is therefore limited, and the paper itself concedes that the practical implications of the VP/EDM difference 'remain an open question'.

The connection between entropy-production peaks and semantic commitment in real models is only qualitative. There is no quantitative validation of the posterior-tracking estimator (Algorithm 1) against ground truth in a setting where the true entropy is known (e.g., synthetic mixtures run through the same estimation pipeline), despite acknowledged calibration-related biases in the local likelihood increments.

The 'entropy' being estimated is not the plain conditional entropy: choosing p(π)=0.5 makes the quantity a Jensen–Shannon divergence, and using the unconditional model as a proxy for the class complement introduces an unquantified bias. The paper discusses these issues but never measures their magnitude.

The empirical evidence rests on a small number of hand-selected classes and prompt pairs ('tiger shark', 'eft', 'paintbrush'; a handful of chair/car/cat prompts). The authors admit they chose prompts by verifying by hand that SD 1.5 follows them, which raises concerns about selection effects; only two relatively small/older models are studied.

The claim that guidance 'redistributes semantic information' is supported only by entropy-profile shifts plus visual inspection of a few image grids; no direct measurement ties the entropy shift to changes in specific semantic attributes, so the causal interpretation remains suggestive rather than established.

Several presentation issues reduce rigor: Eq. (9) is introduced but seemingly unused in the main text; the statement about EDM speciation scaling as a power d^α is left vague (footnote only specifies σ₁=t, t_s=√d); and the difference between forward-time and reverse-time estimation of the entropy is justified only informally in Appendix B.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: it proposes an operational, estimable quantity (class-conditional entropy and its temporal derivative) that connects the statistical-physics 'speciation' picture (Biroli et al., Raya & Ambrogioni) to something measurable in trained diffusion models.

The appendix derivation (A.1–A.2) is clean and self-contained, and the VP-case asymptotic result t_s = (1/2) log d + O(1) correctly recovers the speciation time scale from Biroli et al. (2024), with the rescaled-time collapse in Figure 2c being convincing evidence for the Gaussian mixture setting.

The evaluation spans synthetic mixtures, EDM2-XS on ImageNet-512, and Stable Diffusion 1.5, and the empirical observation of class-dependent entropy profiles (e.g., 'tiger shark' vs 'paintbrush') and prompt-attribute experiments in Section 5.3 are interesting qualitative results.
The limitations section is honest about estimator calibration issues, the unconditional-proxy bias for class complements, and the coarse granularity of SD 1.5.
weaknesses: There is a fundamental mismatch between the theory and the headline experiments. The sharp phase-transition/speciation link (the paper's central theoretical claim) is proven only for the VP process; the authors themselves show in Appendix A.2.3 that for VE/EDM there is NO sharp transition in rescaled time. Yet the main validation uses EDM2-XS (EDM schedule) and SD 1.5 (latent diffusion), i.e., precisely the settings where the theory's key prediction fails. The 'empirically, most classes exhibit a similar unimodal profile' observation is thus not strong evidence for the theoretical claim, and the paper does not confront this gap head-on.

The practical contribution is largely diagnostic and confirmatory. The guidance-distortion analysis (Figure 3) essentially re-confirms the known empirical finding that guidance is beneficial only in a limited noise interval (Kynkäanniemi et al., 2024), without deriving any new actionable method, scheduler, or control rule. The claim of a 'principled basis for time-localized control' is aspirational rather than demonstrated.

Novelty is incremental. The posterior-tracking estimator is taken from Koulischer et al. (2025a), and the partitioned class-conditional entropy is effectively a Jensen-Shannon divergence between two conditional marginals (as the authors admit in Appendix B). The theoretical result for Gaussian mixtures is a straightforward calculation from known posterior decompositions. The paper's value is in the synthesis, not in new machinery.

Key methodological choices are approximations with unclear error impact: using the unconditional model as a proxy for the class complement (Section 5.2, Appendix B), ignoring the p(π) reweighting by choosing p(π)=0.5, and cross-entropy substitution under guidance. No quantitative validation of the estimator against a ground truth is provided (the forward-direction estimator in Appendix B that could serve as a check was explicitly opted against).

The distinction between the two speciation regimes (VP vs EDM) is acknowledged to be of 'unclear practical significance' and deferred to future work, yet it directly undermines the paper's own experimental design; the theoretical section and the experimental section read as somewhat disconnected.

Reproducibility is uncertain: no code release is mentioned, the number of classes sampled, the specific binary partitions used beyond three highlighted classes, and the sample counts for the broad percentile summaries in Figure 3 are not fully specified.

Presentation issues reduce polish: multiple typos ('termporal', 'uni modal', 'SDEs is shown in figure 5', inconsistent capitalization), Equation (8)'s constant factors are hard to trace (g_t^2/2 vs the appendix's factor of 1/2), and Algorithm 1's indexing (H_tau:0 vs I_(y)_(tau-1:0)) is sloppy.

strengths: The paper provides a genuinely useful bridge between the statistical physics literature on speciation/symmetry breaking in diffusion (Biroli et al., 2024; Raya & Ambrogioni, 2023) and an operational, estimable quantity in trained models: the class-conditional entropy and its temporal derivative. The theory result that the entropy transition localizes at ts = (1/2) log d in VP diffusion, matching the speciation time of Biroli et al. (2024), is clean and well-derived (Appendix A provides a complete asymptotic argument).

The distinction between VP and VE/EDM kernels is a valuable negative result: the sharp entropy transition exists for VP but broadens as sqrt(d) for EDM. This is honestly reported (including the admission that the practical significance is unclear) and visualized in Figure 5.

The partitioned class-conditional entropy (Eq. 17) is a sensible and practically motivated refinement that overcomes the insensitivity of the global entropy to hierarchical semantic structure, enabling probing of specific class distinctions and prompt attributes.

Experiments span both a class-conditional model (EDM2-XS on ImageNet-512) and a text-conditioned model (Stable Diffusion 1.5), and the guidance analysis (Figure 3) connects entropy redistribution to independently optimized guidance intervals (FID vs FD_DINOv2), yielding results consistent with Kynkäniemi et al. (2024).

The limitations section is candid: bias from the unconditional-model proxy for the class complement, calibration sensitivity of the posterior updates, and SD 1.5's weak prompt adherence are all acknowledged, and a failure case is explicitly illustrated (Figure 16).
weaknesses: The central claim that entropy 'consistently isolates the noise regimes critical for semantic structure formation' in trained models is supported largely by qualitative evidence. On EDM2-XS and SD 1.5 there is no ground-truth notion of speciation time; agreement is assessed visually (Figures 1, 4, 12–15) via hand-picked classes/prompts that the authors themselves verified by hand for prompt adherence (Appendix C.2). A quantitative validation—e.g., correlating entropy peak locations with measurable attribute emergence across many prompts/classes—is missing.

The estimator introduces several approximations (unconditional model as complement proxy, p(π) = 0.5 reweighting making the quantity effectively a Jensen–Shannon divergence, posterior updates from local likelihood increments) whose combined bias on the reported profiles is not quantified. The main-text interpretation changes subtly between 'entropy' and 'JSD-like overlap of prompt conditionals', which complicates comparison with the theory of Section 4.

The theoretical analysis is confined to equiprobable Gaussian mixtures with strict high-dimensional scaling assumptions (‖µi − µk‖²/d = O(1), σ0 = O(1)); the Appendix A derivation of Eq. (8) is a fairly standard manipulation. Real-data claims therefore rest on a considerable extrapolation from the toy model.

Novelty is moderate: the core estimable quantity builds directly on the posterior-tracking machinery of Koulischer et al. (2025a), and the entropy/information-flow perspective on diffusion is well developed (Kong et al., 2023; Ambrogioni, 2025b; Premkumar, 2025). The main contribution is the connection to the speciation picture plus the partitioned variant, which is useful but incremental.

The abstract's claim of providing 'a principled basis for time-localized control' overstates the contribution: the paper analyzes how guidance distorts entropy relative to pre-existing FID/FD-optimal intervals (from Kynkäniemi et al., 2024) but does not propose or validate any new control mechanism or actionable procedure that uses the diagnostic.

Some presentation issues reduce clarity: the EDM/VE significance discussion is left unresolved, key experimental claims rely on few highlighted classes (tiger shark, eft, paintbrush) with 300 samples for most profiles, and referencing a concurrent submission ('Premkumar, 2026, ICLR 2026 Conference Submission') is unusual and should be better integrated.

strengths: The paper provides an exact, elegant identity (Eqs. 8, 33-35, 42) expressing class-conditional entropy production as a sum of pairwise terms combining posterior competition and score separation, giving a transparent mechanistic account of when information about class semantics is produced during denoising.

The VP vs. VE-EDM analysis is genuinely informative: it shows entropy production concentrates in an O(1) window around t_s = (1/2) log d for VP (matching Biroli et al.'s speciation time) but broadens over O(sqrt(d)) in physical time for VE-EDM, with a clear summary (Table 1) and supporting simulations (Figs. 2, 5, 6).

The practical estimator is developed with unusual care: bias is explicitly decomposed into balanced-prior, unconditional-model-proxy, and posterior-approximation components (Eq. 111, Fig. 7) and validated both in Gaussian mixtures and on EDM2-XS (Fig. 8), with a convergence analysis over sample counts and seeds.

The empirical findings are substantive: class-dependent speciation windows (tiger shark vs. paintbrush), the demonstration that limited-interval guidance redistributes entropy production toward high-noise regimes, and the coarse-to-fine temporal ordering of attribute emergence in Stable Diffusion, all consistent with and quantitatively extending Kynkäänniemi et al. (2024).

The limitations section is honest and specific (calibration sensitivity, unconditional-model bias, SD 1.5 prompt-adherence failures shown explicitly in Fig. 13), and failure modes are documented rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The theoretical novelty is incremental relative to concurrent work. The Gaussian-mixture analysis is a fairly direct application of known speciation scalings (Biroli et al., 2024), and Appendix A.4 largely transcribes the framework and even the large-t expansions (Eqs. 86-90) from Achilli et al. (2026), whose general speciation times already imply the peak-location claim; the paper's addition is connecting these to entropy production, which is close in spirit to Stancević & Ambrogioni (2026).

The central empirical claim that entropy production 'reliably' localizes speciation in trained models rests largely on qualitative evidence (profile shapes, visual inspection of denoised predictions). There is no independent, quantitative validation in trained models that the entropy-production peak coincides with an externally measured semantic-commitment time (e.g., classifier accuracy or sampler-based commitment statistics), and no error bars on the class-dependent window locations.

There is an inherent risk of triviality in the diagnostic: H(Z|X_t) must rise from ~0 to log K as t increases, so its derivative is necessarily nonzero in intermediate regimes; the informative content (localization and class-dependence) is shown, but the paper does not clearly quantify how sharp or how much more than a generic sigmoid transition the profiles are.

The abstract and conclusion promise 'a principled basis for time-localized control,' but no control experiment is performed: guidance intervals are taken from prior work (Kynkääänniemi et al., 2024) and only analyzed post hoc; the intervention study is thus diagnostic rather than prescriptive.

Several foundational references are concurrent or unpublished 2026 preprints (Achilli et al., 2026; Stancević et al., 2026; Premkumar, 2026), making it difficult to assess the delta over the closest related work from the manuscript alone; no code release is stated, which limits reproducibility of the estimator on trained models.

The estimator's accuracy in trained models depends on score calibration across noise levels, and while the bias analysis covers Gaussian mixtures and three EDM2-XS classes, the generalization of the bias conclusions to the full 1K-class ImageNet setting and to text-conditioned models is asserted rather than demonstrated.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well organized, with a thorough related-work section that correctly positions the contribution relative to both the statistical-physics line (Biroli et al., Raya & Ambrogioni, Achilli et al.) and the information-theoretic line (Kong et al., Stancevic & Ambrogioni, Premkumar).

The entropy-production identity (Eqs. 8/35) is correct and provides an interpretable decomposition: entropy production is driven by the joint presence of posterior ambiguity and score separation, and the accompanying asymptotic analysis (Appendix A) is careful, including honest discussion of why the VP transition sharpens while the VE-EDM transition broadens (Table 1, Figure 2).

The partitioned class-conditional entropy (Section 4.5) is a sensible refinement that resolves which semantic distinction drives a given entropy increase, and the bias decomposition of the practical estimator (Appendix B, Eqs. 111, Figures 7-8) shows genuine effort to quantify approximations.

Experiments span both a class-conditional model (EDM2-XS on ImageNet-512) and a text-conditional model (SD 1.5 / SDXL), with reasonable experimental details, sample-size discussion, compute costs, and an honest limitations section covering estimator bias, prompt-adherence failure modes (Figure 13), and the guidance-analysis gap.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty. The core identity follows from standard manipulations of the score mixture decomposition (cf. Kong et al. 2023), and the main asymptotic result (Eq. 19-20, ts(d) = 1/2 log d + O(1)) recovers the speciation scale already established by Biroli et al. (2024). The extension in Section 4.4 / A.4 is largely an application of the speciation framework of Achilli et al. (2026) to the authors' observable, rather than a new theoretical development; overlap with the concurrent Stancevic & Ambrogioni (2026) information-dynamics work is not clearly delineated.

A gap between claims and evidence. The abstract and conclusion promise 'a principled basis for time-localized control,' and Section 5.2 claims the guidance delta 'suggests how guidance can accelerate speciation,' but the paper never uses the entropy diagnostic to choose or act on a guidance interval. The intervals in Figure 3 are instead found by grid search over FID / FD_DINOv2, so the practical utility of the proposed diagnostic for control remains unverified, despite this being the stated motivation ('practical methods to detect and exploit these windows... are still limited').

Validation on trained models is largely qualitative. For EDM2-XS and SD 1.5, the key evidence is that entropy-production profiles peak in intermediate noise regimes and vary plausibly across classes/attributes; there is no ground-truth speciation time against which the peaks can be quantitatively assessed, no error bars on the main profiles (300 samples per class complement; derivative obtained by smoothing + interpolation, acknowledged as high-variance), and the findings essentially restate known time-localized structure claims (Kynkanniemi et al. 2024; Sclocchi et al. 2025) in a new observable.

The practical estimator changes the quantity being measured. Replacing class-complement models with the unconditional model and re-balancing priors converts the conditional entropy into a Jensen-Shannon-type separability measure (Eq. 104) and, under guidance, a cross-entropy (Appendix B). The claim that these substitutions 'do not compromise its quality as an operational measure of speciation' is asserted based on synthetic 200-class mixtures; no formal argument is given that the balanced-prior JSD peak coincides with speciation in general.

Theory-to-practice gap is not bridged. The sharp concentration results hold for isotropic Gaussian mixtures under strict high-dimensional scaling assumptions; nothing in the paper demonstrates that the O(1) window prediction transfers quantitatively to EDM2-XS or SD, where the observed peaks are broad and class-dependent. The authors themselves concede the practical significance of the VP/VE distinction is 'currently unclear.'

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is stated, several key settings (smoothing kernel, posterior-update hyperparameters, partition choices for SD prompts) are only loosely specified, and prompt selection for SD 1.5 was manually curated, which weakens the generality of the coarse-to-fine ordering claim in Section 5.3.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated connection between information theory and the statistical-physics picture of diffusion: the closed-form entropy-production identity (Eq. 8/35) makes explicit that speciation peaks arise from the joint presence of posterior ambiguity and score separation, which is an insightful mechanistic explanation.

The theoretical analysis is solid for the solvable case: the VP/VE-EDM comparison (sharp O(1) window at t_s = (1/2)log d vs. a broadening O(√d) window) is a genuinely novel and non-obvious observation, and the derivation matches the speciation times of Biroli et al. (2024) and generalizes to the framework of Achilli et al. (2026), including covariance-distinguished classes.
The partitioned class-conditional entropy is a simple and useful construct that resolves semantic decisions at different abstraction levels, which the full class entropy cannot.

Practical relevance is demonstrated on real trained models (EDM2-XS on ImageNet-512, SD 1.5/SDXL on LAION), including a quantitative guidance analysis that connects entropy redistribution to known guidance pathologies (Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024).

Reproducibility treatment is above average: Algorithm 1 is specified, computational costs are reported, estimator bias is decomposed and studied empirically (Eqs. 111, Figures 7-8), and sample counts, samplers, and metrics are documented in detail.

The limitations section is honest and specific, identifying posterior-calibration bias, the unconditional-proxy approximation, and SD 1.5's weak prompt adherence as concrete concerns rather than generic caveats.
weaknesses: Validation in trained models is largely qualitative and circular: the claim that entropy peaks 'isolate the noise regimes critical for semantic structure formation' is supported mainly by visual inspection of denoised predictions (Figures 1, 4, 12) rather than by any quantitative agreement with an independent ground truth for when semantics emerge, so the central empirical claim rests on interpretive judgment.

The paper's framing promises 'a principled basis for time-localized control,' but no intervention experiment is performed: the guidance analysis (Figure 3) is descriptive of how entropy production shifts, and the paper never shows that acting on the entropy signal (e.g., scheduling guidance from measured entropy peaks) improves sample quality or FID/FD. The gap between diagnostic and control is acknowledged only in passing.

The theoretical guarantees hold under strong assumptions (isotropic Gaussian kernels, high-dimensional mean/covariance scaling, self-averaging Pure Density Decompositions) that plausibly fail for image data; the bridge from theory to practice is by analogy, and no experiment tests the predicted scaling laws (e.g., the √d VE window) on real models.

The practical estimator deviates from the theory in non-trivial ways (balanced priors converting the quantity into a JSD-type separability measure, unconditional model as complement proxy, posterior approximation), and the authors' own bias analysis (Figure 7) shows the strongest bias comes from prior re-balancing and that profile shape is altered even if peak location is not; downstream uses sensitive to shape may inherit this bias.

Incremental originality relative to very recent and concurrent work: the entropy-production identity builds directly on Koulischer et al. (2025a) for the estimator and Achilli et al. (2026) for the speciation framework, and entropy/information-flow views of diffusion are already established (Stancevic & Ambrogioni, 2026; Premkumar, 2025/2026; Kong et al., 2023); the novel part is essentially the speciation-peak correspondence and the partitioned probe.

The VE-EDM finding (transition does not sharpen with dimension) is reported as an unexplained observation whose 'practical significance is unclear,' and the guidance-induced redistribution is not connected to any predictive or prescriptive claim, leaving two of the paper's headline directions incomplete.

Text-conditioned experiments use a small set of hand-curated prompts verified for prompt adherence (Figures 4, 13-17), raising selection-bias concerns about how representative the coarse-to-fine ordering is across the prompt distribution.
